entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Nasir Khusraw (c. 1004 – c. 1088 CE), born Abu Mu'in al-Din Nasir ibn Khusraw al-Qubadiyani al-Marwazi, emerged from the culturally vibrant Khurasan region of Persia as a towering figure of 11th-century Islamic thought. A polymath, his life trajectory dramatically shifted from a comfortable position in the Seljuk administration to an ardent Isma'ili missionary (da'i) and philosopher, profoundly influencing Persian literature and esoteric Islamic theology. His intellectual journey, marked by a seven-year pilgrimage across the Islamic world, positioned him as a critical conduit for Fatimid Isma'ili doctrines into Central Asia, challenging prevailing Sunni orthodoxies and shaping the intellectual landscape of the eastern Islamic lands.

After a profound spiritual awakening during his Hajj pilgrimage from 1046 to 1052 CE, which included an extended stay in Cairo, the capital of the Fatimid Caliphate, Nasir Khusraw embraced the Isma'ili branch of Shi'ism. He was subsequently appointed a Fatimid da'i (missionary) and returned to his native Khurasan, where he faced intense persecution from the Seljuk authorities and Sunni religious establishment. His literary output during this period was prolific, encompassing philosophical treatises like the *Jami' al-Hikmatayn* (The Confluence of the Two Wisdoms), which sought to reconcile ancient Greek philosophy with Isma'ili cosmology, and the *Safarnama*, a vivid travelogue detailing his journey from Merv to Mecca and Cairo, offering invaluable insights into 11th-century Islamic societies.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nasir Khusraw's profound philosophical and poetic works fundamentally shaped Persian literature and ensured the intellectual continuity of Isma'ili thought, particularly in Central Asia, by synthesizing diverse intellectual traditions. His *Safarnama* also provides unparalleled firsthand accounts of 11th-century Islamic societies.
